messages.content: You are a careful taxonomist of writing-assessment constructs. Output only valid JSON matching the requested schema.

You are consolidating evaluation criteria discovered independently by several LLM judges into a set of shared constructs.

Each judge compared the same student argumentative essays, all written in response to one source-based prompt and, with no fixed
rubric, named the qualities that distinguished the stronger essay. Each judge's raw phrasings
have already been canonicalized separately, so within a single judge the criteria below are
already distinct from one another. Your job is to identify, ACROSS judges, which criteria denote
the same underlying construct.

Below is the full list. Each entry has an INDEX in square brackets, the JUDGE that produced it,
its NAME, and a one-sentence DEFINITION.

[0] (gpt-5.4-mini) Organization: Arranges the essay into clear parts or paragraphs that give the argument a recognizable structure.
[1] (gpt-5.4-mini) Use of source evidence: Uses details from the source text as evidence and ties them to the essay's claims.
[2] (gpt-5.4-mini) Thesis clarity and control: States a clear arguable position and maintains that position as the controlling focus of the essay.
[3] (gpt-5.4-mini) Elaboration: Expands claims beyond bare assertion by explaining and elaborating reasons or evidence in fuller detail.
[4] (gpt-5.4-mini) Conclusion: Provides an effective ending that closes the essay by restating or synthesizing the main claim and reasons.
[5] (gpt-5.4-mini) Counterargument handling: Acknowledges opposing views or objections and responds to them within the argument.
[6] (gpt-5.4-mini) Analytical reasoning: Explains how or why evidence leads to claims through analysis, causal logic, or explicit reasoning.
[7] (gpt-5.4-mini) Argument depth: Engages the issue at a deeper level by addressing broader implications, complexities, or substantive consequences.
[8] (gpt-5.4-mini) Sentence-level control: Shows readable, controlled sentence-level writing through clear wording, smoother fluency, and fewer distracting errors.
[9] (gpt-5.4-mini) Nuanced stance: Presents a balanced or qualified judgment that weighs both sides, sets conditions, or avoids an overly absolute stance.
[10] (gpt-5.4-mini) Specificity: Makes the argument concrete and vivid through specific examples, details, or particularized consequences.
[11] (gpt-5.4-mini) Rhetorical force: Uses assertive, engaging, or emphatic language to make the argument feel more persuasive and forceful.
[12] (gpt-5.4-mini) Relevance: Keeps claims, reasons, and evidence closely tied to the prompt, source, and specific argument being made.
[13] (gpt-5.4-mini) Introductory framing: Opens by setting up the issue, hooking the reader, or framing the topic as a debate worth arguing.
[14] (gpt-5.4-mini) Formal tone: Maintains an appropriately academic, essay-like register rather than a casual or conversational one.
[15] (claude-haiku-4.5) Organization and Structural Coherence: Arranges ideas, paragraphs, and transitions in a logical structure that guides the reader through the argument.
[16] (claude-haiku-4.5) Evidence Integration and Textual Support: Selects relevant source evidence and weaves it purposefully into the writer's own argument as support.
[17] (claude-haiku-4.5) Logical Reasoning and Explanation: Explains how and why claims, evidence, causes, and consequences connect through sound reasoning.
[18] (claude-haiku-4.5) Counterargument Engagement: Acknowledges, addresses, and responds to opposing views or objections.
[19] (claude-haiku-4.5) Mechanics, Grammar, and Sentence Control: Maintains readable, correct sentences and control of spelling, grammar, punctuation, and other writing mechanics.
[20] (claude-haiku-4.5) Argument Focus and Thesis: States a clear central position and maintains that focus consistently throughout the essay.
[21] (claude-haiku-4.5) Nuance, Complexity, and Broader Implications: Shows sophisticated, balanced thinking by recognizing complexity, limits, and wider implications beyond a simplistic yes/no view.
[22] (claude-haiku-4.5) Argument Development and Breadth: Builds a substantive case by elaborating points and developing multiple supporting reasons or dimensions.
[23] (claude-haiku-4.5) Conclusion Effectiveness and Closure: Provides a purposeful ending that synthesizes the argument and reinforces the thesis.
[24] (claude-haiku-4.5) Concrete Illustration and Specificity: Makes claims tangible and precise through specific examples, scenarios, technical details, or clearly identified problems.
[25] (claude-haiku-4.5) Source Understanding and Engagement: Demonstrates substantive comprehension of the source text's key issues, complexities, and distinctions and uses that understanding to engage the prompt.
[26] (claude-haiku-4.5) Contextual Framing and Introduction: Frames the topic with relevant background or a strong opening that situates and launches the argument.
[27] (claude-haiku-4.5) Style, Register, and Voice: Uses an appropriate argumentative tone and a mature, effective command of voice, diction, and sentence style.
[28] (claude-haiku-4.5) Rhetorical Effectiveness and Audience Engagement: Uses rhetorical devices or audience awareness to make the argument more engaging or persuasive.
[29] (claude-haiku-4.5) Task Fulfillment and Completeness: Meets the assignment's basic expectations by fully completing the essay and adhering to the prompt or required format.
[30] (claude-haiku-4.5) Accurate Source Representation: Faithfully and precisely represents the source text's content, quotations, and citations without distortion.
[31] (gemini-3.6-flash) Source Evidence Integration: Captures how effectively the essay selects, incorporates, and synthesizes details from the source text to support its argument.
[32] (gemini-3.6-flash) Reasoning and Elaboration: Captures the depth with which the essay develops claims by analyzing evidence, explaining implications, and extending ideas beyond surface summary.
[33] (gemini-3.6-flash) Conventions and Mechanics: Captures control of standard written English, including grammar, spelling, punctuation, usage, and sentence-level correctness.
[34] (gemini-3.6-flash) Thesis and Stance: Captures how clearly, explicitly, and consistently the essay states and maintains its central argumentative position.
[35] (gemini-3.6-flash) Cohesion and Transitions: Captures how smoothly ideas are linked across sentences and paragraphs through transitions, connectors, and flowing progression.
[36] (gemini-3.6-flash) Focus and Task Relevance: Measures whether the essay stays on topic, addresses the prompt directly, and avoids irrelevant digressions.
[37] (deepseek-v4-flash) Organization and Coherence: Arranges the essay and its paragraphs into a clear, logically connected structure with effective progression and transitions.
[38] (deepseek-v4-flash) Reasoning Development: Builds the case through fully developed, substantive, and logically connected reasons rather than brief or repetitive assertions.
[39] (deepseek-v4-flash) Counterargument and Nuance: Acknowledges opposing views and complexity, weighing them to produce a more balanced or qualified argument.
[40] (deepseek-v4-flash) Thesis and Focus: States a clear argumentative position and keeps the essay consistently focused on that stance and the assigned task.
[41] (deepseek-v4-flash) Written Language Control: Demonstrates control of grammar, spelling, mechanics, sentence formation, and clarity so the prose is readable and correct.
[42] (deepseek-v4-flash) Analytical Depth: Moves beyond surface summary to draw inferences, examine implications, and contribute independent critical thinking.
[43] (deepseek-v4-flash) Conclusion Effectiveness: Ends with a coherent, purposeful conclusion that reinforces and synthesizes the argument.
[44] (deepseek-v4-flash) Formal Register: Maintains an appropriately formal, measured, school-appropriate tone for argumentative writing.
[45] (deepseek-v4-flash) Rhetorical Effectiveness: Uses voice, audience awareness, framing, and other rhetorical devices to make the argument engaging and persuasive.
[46] (deepseek-v4-flash) Language Sophistication: Uses mature, precise vocabulary and varied syntax to create a more sophisticated academic prose style.

Instructions:
- Group entries that denote the SAME underlying evaluative construct, judging by MEANING, not by
  surface wording. Different words for the same idea belong in one group; the same word used for
  different ideas belongs in different groups.
- Keep genuinely DISTINCT constructs separate, even when related. Two constructs a writing expert
  would score on separate rubric lines should be separate groups.
- A group may contain AT MOST ONE criterion per judge. The criteria within a judge were already
  canonicalized, so two of them never denote the same construct; if you find yourself wanting to
  place two criteria from one judge together, they belong in different groups.
- A criterion with no counterpart in any other judge forms a group of ONE. Do not absorb it into a
  loosely related group to tidy up, and do not create a catch-all: a construct only one judge
  discovered is a real finding and must stand alone.
- Do NOT try to balance the groups. There is no target number of groups and no expectation that
  every group contains every judge. Groups of one, two, three, and four are all equally valid
  outcomes; forcing coverage would fabricate agreement that is not there.
- Do NOT merge two constructs just because they often co-occur or because strong essays tend to
  score well on both. Group only by shared MEANING.
- The judge labels are present only so you can respect the one-per-judge rule. They carry no
  information about meaning; never group or split on the basis of which judge produced an entry.

For each group, give:
- a canonical NAME: a concise noun phrase naming the single construct the group captures. Name the
  construct itself, not the union of its members' wordings; avoid conjunctions unless the construct
  genuinely has no single name.
- a one-sentence DEFINITION of that construct.
- the list of members, each as its INDEX, its JUDGE, and its NAME copied verbatim.

Rules on membership (these will be checked programmatically):
- Every input index must appear in exactly one group, exactly once. Place all of them; drop none;
  duplicate none.
- Do not invent indices that are not in the input.
- Each member's "judge" and "name" must be the exact input values at that index -- this is a
  cross-check, so copy them from the bracketed entry, do not paraphrase.
- No group may contain two members with the same judge.

Output only JSON:
{"clusters": [{"name": "<canonical noun phrase>", "definition": "<one sentence>",
"members": [{"index": <int>, "judge": "<verbatim>", "name": "<verbatim>"}, ...]}, ...]}
